title: Normed and Banach spaces
summary: Why infinite dimensions need new machinery; norms and the metric they induce; the sup norm, ℓ^p and C_∞(X); completeness and the first Banach spaces; the first failure of a finite-dimensional comfort: norm equivalence.

objectives.description: State the norm axioms and verify them for the sup norm on C_∞(X).
Explain why convergence in the sup norm is uniform convergence and why C_∞(X) is complete.
Show by explicit computation that the sup norm and the integral norm on C([0,1]) are not equivalent, and name the finite-dimensional hypothesis that fails.
Produce a Cauchy sequence in (C([0,1]), ‖·‖₁) with no continuous limit.

preparation.description: Read lecture 1 notes, pages 1–5: vector spaces, finite versus infinite dimension (the x^n example), the norm axioms and the induced metric.
Read the sup norm on C_∞(X) (Definition 10, Proposition 11) and the definition of ℓ^p (Definition 12).
Read Definition 14 (Banach space) and Theorem 16 with its proof; note the three-step pattern: candidate limit, candidate in the space, convergence in norm.

commonMisconceptions.claim: All norms on a vector space are equivalent, so the choice of norm on C([0,1]) does not matter.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Equivalence of all norms is a theorem about finite-dimensional spaces. On C([0,1]) the sequence x^n has sup norm 1 and integral norm 1/(n+1); no constant C gives ‖f‖_∞ ≤ C‖f‖₁.

commonMisconceptions.claim: Convergence in the integral norm implies pointwise convergence.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It does not: the functions can converge to 0 in ‖·‖₁ while taking the value 1 somewhere for every n (narrow spikes). The sup norm, by contrast, controls every point.

commonMisconceptions.claim: A closed and bounded subset of a Banach space is compact.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Heine–Borel fails in infinite dimensions; the notes flag this at the outset. The unit ball of ℓ^p is closed and bounded but not compact.
